newsitem.title: USA: Norfolk argues agains Conrail in appeal.
newsitem.headline: Norfolk argues agains Conrail in appeal.

text.p: A three-judge federal court panel adjourned with no ruling Tuesday after hearing Norfolk Southern Corp.'s appeal of a lower court ruling that refused to block provisions that protect the proposed merger between Conrail Inc. and CSX Corp.

Norfolk Southern's attorney, Steven Rothschild, said that by granting CSX options on millions of shares, and by allowing CSX to vote its 19.9 percent of Conrail's stock, Conrail was "impermissably delegating" and "inappropriately abdicating" the responsibility of its current board to a third party -- CSX.

He also said the exclusivity provision in the deal between Conrail and CSX, which prohibits Conrail from seeking or accepting any other mergers until 1999, was coercive to Conrail's stockholders and allows Conrail and CSX to tinker with their pact until they succeed./

The longer CSX and Conrail have, the greater the chances for a vote by Conrail shareholders to exempt Conrail from a Pennsylvania law that would require CSX to pay all cash for Conrail, Rothschild said.

In a session that lasted just over an hour, the judges heard arguments from attorneys representing all three railroad giants, as well as from an attorney trying a class action suit brought by some Conrail shareholders who allege Conrail's recommendation of CSX's tender offer inadequately disclosed the full value of Conrail's stock.
Norfolk's appeal and the class-action suit were consolidated by the Third Circuit Court of Appeals here.
Norfolk Southern has started a hostile takeover of Conrail by offering $115 per share in cash for all of Conrail's stock, a deal valued at about $10.3 billion.

CSX has offered $110 per share in cash for up to 40 percent of Conrail's stock, and has offered CSX stock for the remaining 60 percent, in a deal valued at about $1 billion less than Norfolk Southern's offer.

Theodore Mirvis, arguing on behalf of CSX, said the exclusivity period did not present irreparable harm to the legal rights of Norfolk Southern, and that Pennsylvania's merger laws allowed Conrail's board to impose the restriction.
Conrail's attorney, Thomas Van Kirk, said Conrail's board took appropriate action to prevent the company from being raided by both Norfolk Southern and CSX.

Van Kirk said negotiations in 1994 between Conrail and Norfolk Southern failed to bring about a stock-swap merger. "It was then in 1995 that Norfolk Southern and CSX got together to decided whether to carve up Conrail," he said.

Conrail, after 1995, "entered into strategic planning negotiations ... and what they decided to do is to enter into a strategic merger with CSX. They had the right to do that and were fulfilling their fiduciary duties," Van Kirk said, adding, "To this day, Norfolk Southern has never made a merger proposal to Conrail's board of directors."
The court is expected to issue a decision in six to eight weeks.
